# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is a cornerstone of sudden cardiac death prevention in patients at risk for life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias [1]. Conventional transvenous ICDs (TV-ICDs), although highly effective, carry well-documented risks related to the intravascular leads, including lead fracture, venous occlusion, and systemic infection requiring complex lead extraction [2,3]. The subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) was developed to circumvent these lead-related complications by avoiding intravascular and intracardiac placement entirely [4]. Since its first clinical descriptions and regulatory approval (CE mark in 2009 and FDA approval in 2012), the S-ICD has become an established alternative for selected patients [5].

## Device Design and Function

The S-ICD system consists of a pulse generator implanted in a lateral or intermuscular pocket and a single subcutaneous lead positioned parasternally [4,6]. Unlike TV-ICDs, the S-ICD does not provide long-term bradycardia pacing, antitachycardia pacing (ATP), or cardiac resynchronization therapy, although it can deliver transient post-shock pacing [6]. Sensing relies on surface-like electrograms across three available vectors, with an automated screening process performed before implantation to ensure adequate signal quality and minimize inappropriate detection [7]. The device delivers an 80-J shock for terminating ventricular arrhythmias, with high reported conversion efficacy [8].

## Clinical Efficacy and Evidence

Early experience was established in the IDE study and the EFFORTLESS registry, which demonstrated reliable arrhythmia conversion and acceptable complication rates in real-world cohorts [8,9]. Pooled analyses confirmed high rates of successful conversion of induced and spontaneous ventricular arrhythmias [10]. The landmark PRAETORIAN trial, a randomized comparison of S-ICD versus TV-ICD, demonstrated non-inferiority of the S-ICD for the composite endpoint of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [11]. This trial provided the strongest evidence supporting the S-ICD as a viable alternative for patients who do not require pacing [11]. The UNTOUCHED study further evaluated inappropriate shock rates in a primary-prevention population with reduced ejection fraction, reporting low inappropriate shock rates with contemporary programming [12].

## Patient Selection

The S-ICD is particularly attractive for younger patients, those with limited vascular access, patients with prior device infections, and individuals at high risk of bacteremia, such as those on hemodialysis [13,14]. It is also favored in patients with congenital heart disease and channelopathies such as Brugada syndrome and long QT syndrome, where pacing is rarely required [15,16]. Guidelines from professional societies endorse the S-ICD as a Class IIa recommendation in patients with an indication for an ICD who do not need pacing therapy [1,17]. Conversely, the S-ICD is unsuitable for patients requiring bradycardia pacing, ATP for monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, or resynchronization [17].

## Complications and Limitations

While the S-ICD avoids intravascular complications, it is not free of adverse events. Inappropriate shocks—frequently due to T-wave oversensing—were a notable early concern, though refinements in sensing algorithms and dual-zone programming have substantially reduced their incidence [12,18]. Device-related infections, although typically more superficial than transvenous system infections, still occur and may necessitate extraction [19]. Other concerns include the larger generator size, premature battery depletion in early models, and the absence of pacing capabilities [20,21]. Screening failure prior to implantation excludes a subset of patients due to inadequate sensing vectors [7].

## Integration with Other Technologies

A significant limitation—the lack of ATP—has prompted interest in combining the S-ICD with the leadless pacemaker to create a modular cardiac rhythm management system [22]. The MODULAR ATP study evaluated communication between a leadless pacemaker and the S-ICD, demonstrating feasibility of antitachycardia pacing delivery [23]. Such hybrid approaches may broaden S-ICD eligibility in the future [22,24].

## Special Populations and Long-Term Outcomes

Registry and observational data support favorable outcomes in pediatric and adult congenital heart disease populations [15,25]. Studies in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy patients also report effective therapy delivery [26]. Long-term follow-up from EFFORTLESS and subsequent cohorts confirms durable performance and stable complication rates over several years [27]. Cost-effectiveness analyses suggest that, despite higher upfront device costs, the reduction in lead-related complications may offset expenses over time in appropriately selected patients [28].

## Future Directions

Ongoing innovation focuses on smaller generators, improved battery longevity, enhanced sensing algorithms incorporating machine learning, and seamless integration with leadless pacing technology [21,29]. The evolving evidence base continues to refine patient selection, and emerging data may expand indications as device capabilities mature [30].

## Conclusion

The S-ICD represents an important advance in defibrillation therapy, offering effective protection against sudden cardiac death while avoiding the inherent risks of transvenous leads. With robust randomized evidence and growing clinical experience, it is now firmly established for patients who do not require pacing. Continued technological evolution, particularly integration with leadless pacing, promises to extend its applicability further [11,23,30].
